glossary.definition: A tall, eye-catching landmark placed to pull guests through a space — Walt Disney's nickname for it, after the sausages used to lead a dog.
Making things look bigger, taller or further away by shrinking the parts that are higher up or further back.
A raised earth bank, usually planted, that hides the outside world from the park.
People judge an experience mostly by its most intense moment and its ending, not by its average or length.
A mismatch between what the eyes report and what the inner ear feels; the leading explanation for motion sickness.
Waiting time filled with something to do or look at; it feels shorter than empty time.
A park layout where lands radiate from a central plaza so guests can always return to the middle and pick another direction.
Linear synchronous motor — magnets on the train and powered coils in the track push the train forward without a chain.
Linear induction motor — a launch system that induces current in a metal fin on the train to push it along.
How hard you are being pushed into (or lifted out of) your seat, measured in multiples of normal gravity.
The floating feeling when a coaster crests a hill fast enough that the seat falls away beneath you (negative or near-zero g).
A teardrop-shaped vertical loop whose curve tightens gradually, keeping g-forces comfortable all the way round.
Failure Mode and Effects Analysis — a table of everything that could go wrong, how bad it would be, and how it is prevented.
A section of track that only one train may occupy at a time, enforced by the ride control system.
A Victorian stage trick: a lit figure reflects in a sheet of angled glass so a transparent 'ghost' appears in the scene.
A family of dull greens and greys used to paint things guests are not meant to notice.
The earliest, no-limits idea phase of attraction design before budgets and feasibility narrow things down.
Trimming scope or cost while trying to keep the parts of an experience that matter most.
How many guests an attraction can serve per hour, also called hourly capacity or THRC.
The time between one vehicle leaving the station and the next one leaving.
The 1884 Coney Island gravity ride that is usually called the first American roller coaster.
A live computer model of a ride or park, fed by sensors, used to predict and test changes.
The person who leads an attraction project across creative, engineering and construction teams.
